claims.statement: Godot's asynchronous resource path is ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request(path) to queue the load, load_threaded_get_status(path, progress) to poll, and load_threaded_get(path) to retrieve; the progress array returns a one-element array containing the percentage.
claims.locator: Section 'Using ResourceLoader'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; applies to any platform with threads.

claims.statement: load_threaded_get() blocks like the synchronous load() if the background load has not finished, so a non-blocking loading screen must either poll the status or leave enough time between request and retrieval.
claims.locator: Section 'Using ResourceLoader', paragraph beginning 'Once you call load_threaded_get()'

claims.statement: load_threaded_request exposes use_sub_threads (default false); setting it true uses multiple threads to load a resource, which is faster but may affect the main thread and cause game slowdowns.
claims.locator: Method description for load_threaded_request (use_sub_threads parameter)

claims.statement: ResourceLoader has five cache modes: CACHE_MODE_IGNORE=0, CACHE_MODE_REUSE=1 (default), CACHE_MODE_REPLACE=2, CACHE_MODE_IGNORE_DEEP=3, CACHE_MODE_REPLACE_DEEP=4; the mode decides whether the main resource, subresources and external dependencies are read from and written to the resource cache.
claims.locator: Enum 'CacheMode' and parameter cache_mode of load_threaded_request
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable API reference; value 1 is the documented default.

claims.statement: Threaded loading is only safe under the documented thread rules: resources may be loaded and manipulated on one thread, but the same resource must not be loaded from several threads at once, and the loaded objects must be added to the active scene on the main thread.
claims.locator: Section 'Resources'

claims.statement: Godot 4's global-illumination option set is documented as exactly three techniques - VoxelGI, SDFGI and LightmapGI - alongside reflection probes and a 'Faking global illumination' page, so the engine offers three distinct GI implementations rather than one scalable system.
claims.locator: Page table of contents: 'Introduction to global illumination', 'Using Voxel global illumination', 'Signed distance field global illumination (SDFGI)', 'Using Lightmap global illumination', 'Reflection probes', 'Faking global illumination'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs GI section index; the page is a TOC, so it evidences the option set, not any cost.

claims.statement: Godot 4.0 introduced SDFGI as a new real-time global illumination technique for large open worlds, and replaced the old GIProbe node with the VoxelGI node for small and medium-scale environments.
claims.locator: Section 'Global illumination' of the Godot 4.0 release announcement

claims.statement: VoxelGI and SDFGI are supported only by the Forward+ renderer, not by the Mobile or Compatibility renderers.
claims.locator: Important callout under 'Using Voxel global illumination'; the same restriction is repeated for SDFGI
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; both GI techniques are Forward+-only.

claims.statement: Godot's own documentation ranks SDFGI as 'one of the most demanding global illumination techniques in Godot', and states that raising the Cascades value is 'significantly more expensive on the CPU and GPU', with the cost increasing especially when the camera moves fast; the doc suggests reducing cascades to 4 or lower for fast-moving cameras.
claims.locator: Sections 'Signed distance field global illumination (SDFGI)' and 'Environment SDFGI properties' -> 'Cascades'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs. 'Significantly more expensive' is qualitative; the doc's only number is the recommended cap of 4 cascades.

claims.statement: SDFGI supports dynamic lights but not dynamic occluders or dynamic emissive surfaces, giving it better real-time ability than baked lightmaps but worse than VoxelGI.
claims.locator: First paragraph of 'Signed distance field global illumination (SDFGI)'

claims.statement: For VoxelGI, meshes baked in the default Static mode cannot use custom ShaderMaterial - they are treated as pure black light blockers; the Dynamic GI mode is 'much slower compared to Static' and is recommended only for large meshes that change significantly during gameplay.
claims.locator: Sections 'VoxelGI interaction with lights and objects' and the Note under it

claims.statement: Baked lightmaps 'consume almost no resources at runtime' and work on low-end PCs and mobile devices, but baking runs on the GPU and 'can take several minutes if not more', versus 'a matter of seconds' for a VoxelGI bake; LightmapGI also reserves the UV2 slot of baked materials.
claims.locator: Section 'Using Lightmap global illumination' (intro) and 'Baking lightmaps will also reserve baked materials' UV2 slot'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; bake-time statements are qualitative (seconds vs minutes).

claims.statement: LightmapGI unwrapping on import exposes a 'Lightmap Texel Size' import option whose default is 0.2, suited to small/medium scenes, with 0.5 or more suggested for larger scenes, especially when only indirect light is baked.
claims.locator: Section 'Unwrap on scene import (recommended)' -> 'Meshes > Lightmap Texel Size'

claims.statement: Godot has two 3D particle systems: GPUParticles3D processed on the GPU and CPUParticles3D processed on the CPU; the docs state GPU systems 'can render hundreds of thousands of particles on modern hardware' and support custom particle shaders plus attractor and collision nodes, while CPU particles work on a wider range of hardware but 'can't render as many individual particles'.
claims.locator: Section 'Node overview' -> 'All 3D particle nodes available in Godot'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs. 'Hundreds of thousands' is the documentation's qualitative hardware claim, not a benchmark.

claims.statement: GPUParticles3D defaults are amount = 8, fixed_fps = 30, interpolate = true, fract_delta = true, collision_base_size = 0.01 m, lifetime = 1.0 s, one_shot = false, visibility_aabb = AABB(-4,-4,-4,8,8,8) and MAX_DRAW_PASSES = 4.
claims.locator: Property Descriptions and Constants sections of the GPUParticles3D class reference
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable API reference; these are engine defaults, not tuned production values.

claims.statement: The class reference warns that higher 'amount' increases GPU requirements 'even if not all particles are visible at a given time', and that lowering amount_ratio gives NO performance benefit because resources are allocated and processed for the total amount regardless; changing amount restarts the system, while changing amount_ratio does not.
claims.locator: Property Descriptions for 'amount' and 'amount_ratio'

claims.statement: The effective emission rate is (amount * amount_ratio) / lifetime particles per second.
claims.locator: Property Description for 'amount' ('The effective emission rate is (amount * amount_ratio) / lifetime particles per second.')
claims.context: Derived from the documented formula using the engine's own defaults (amount=8, amount_ratio=1.0, lifetime=1.0 s) to show the shape of the budget; the formula itself is quoted from the docs.

claims.statement: Per-particle behaviour is written in a particle shader with a start() function (runs once when the system starts) and a process() function (runs every frame); TRANSFORM, COLOR and CUSTOM are saved across frames and are readable by the mesh shader, which is how a GPUParticles3D node can drive thousands of independently moving instances.
claims.locator: Section 'Controlling thousands of fish with Particles' (start()/process(), 'A unique thing about particle shaders is that some built-in variables are saved across frames')
claims.context: Primary godot-docs RST source; no FPS numbers are given.

claims.statement: Automatic mesh LOD was introduced in Godot 4.0 ('you can leverage the new automatic mesh LOD'), alongside automatic occlusion culling and manual HLOD via visibility ranges.
claims.locator: Section on occlusion culling / mesh LOD in the Godot 4.0 release announcement

claims.statement: LOD meshes are generated automatically at import time (glTF, .blend, Collada, FBX) using the meshoptimizer library, and are then used automatically at render time; OBJ files only get LOD generation if their Import As option is changed to Scene. Mesh LOD works with MeshInstance3D, MultiMeshInstance3D, GPUParticles3D and CPUParticles3D.
claims.locator: Sections 'Introduction' and 'Generating mesh LOD'

claims.statement: The global switch is Rendering > Mesh LOD > LOD Change > Threshold Pixels, whose default of 1 pixel is described as tuned to look perceptually lossless; higher values move LOD transitions closer and raise performance at lower quality, and each viewport exposes it as mesh_lod_threshold.
claims.locator: Section 'Configuring mesh LOD performance and quality'

claims.statement: Per-object control is the LOD Bias property on any GeometryInstance3D: values above 1.0 delay LOD transitions (higher quality, lower performance), values below 1.0 make them happen sooner.
claims.locator: Section 'Configuring mesh LOD performance and quality' -> 'LOD Bias'

claims.statement: LOD selection uses the point of the node's AABB closest to the camera, so all instances of a MultiMeshInstance3D, CPUParticles3D or GPUParticles3D are drawn at the same LOD level at a given time; the docs advise splitting far-apart instances into separate MultiMeshInstance3D nodes, which also restores per-node frustum and occlusion culling.
claims.locator: Section 'Using mesh LOD with MultiMesh and particles'

claims.statement: The docs warn that LOD generation 'is not perfect, and may occasionally introduce rendering issues (especially in skinned meshes)' and 'can also take a while on complex meshes'; generation can be disabled per mesh in the Import dock, which also speeds up importing.
claims.locator: Note in section 'Generating mesh LOD'

claims.statement: A MultiMesh is a single draw primitive that can draw up to millions of objects in one go, using GPU hardware; it is described as the next step after using servers directly when object counts reach the hundreds of thousands or millions.
claims.locator: Section 'MultiMeshes'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs (page carries a 'Work in progress / not yet updated for Godot 4.7' banner).

claims.statement: There is no screen or frustum culling for individual MultiMesh instances - 'millions of objects will be always or never drawn, depending on the visibility of the whole MultiMesh'. A custom visibility rect can be supplied but visibility remains all-or-none; the documented workaround is several MultiMeshes for different world areas.
claims.locator: Section 'MultiMeshes', paragraph 'The only drawback is that there is no screen or frustum culling...'

claims.statement: MultiMesh.visible_instance_count controls how many instances are drawn; the documented workflow is to allocate the maximum number of instances up front and then change only the visible count as needed, avoiding reallocation.
claims.locator: Section 'MultiMeshes' -> 'the amount of visible ones can be controlled with the MultiMesh.visible_instance_count property'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; this is the documented pooling pattern.

claims.statement: transform_format must be set before instance_count (changing the format is not allowed afterwards); the C++/GDExtension path can set the whole state of all objects in one call with RenderingServer.multimesh_set_buffer(), which the docs note can be built with multiple threads and gives high cache efficiency.
claims.locator: Code example 'extends MultiMeshInstance3D' and the paragraph referencing RenderingServer.multimesh_set_buffer()

claims.statement: MultiMeshInstance3D is documented as 'a specialized node to instance GeometryInstance3Ds based on a MultiMesh resource', which the API reference describes as 'useful to optimize the rendering of a high number of instances of a given mesh (for example trees in a forest or grass strands)' - the engine-level justification for using it instead of many MeshInstance3D nodes.
claims.locator: Class description of MultiMeshInstance3D ('Node that instances a MultiMesh' / 'useful to optimize the rendering of a high number of instances')
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable API reference; qualitative statement only.

claims.statement: Godot's high-level networking is built on a mid-level MultiplayerPeer object (extended from PacketPeer) with shipped implementations based on ENet (ENetMultiplayerPeer), WebRTC (WebRTCMultiplayerPeer) and WebSocket (WebSocketMultiplayerPeer); the default high-level API is SceneTree-based and RPCs are declared with the @rpc annotation.
claims.locator: Sections 'Mid-level abstraction' and 'Remote procedure calls'

claims.statement: The server peer ID is always 1 and clients receive random positive integer IDs; connection lifecycle is observed through the MultiplayerAPI signals peer_connected(id), peer_disconnected(id), connected_to_server(), connection_failed() and server_disconnected().
claims.locator: Section 'Managing connections'

claims.statement: Godot's high-level multiplayer API uses UDP only, so a self-hosted server port must be forwarded in UDP (not just TCP); the docs also note that HTML5 offers WebSockets and WebRTC but lacks raw low-level TCP/UDP and some higher-level features.
claims.locator: Section 'Hosting considerations' and the preceding Note on platform support

claims.statement: ENetMultiplayerPeer.create_server(port, max_clients = 32, max_channels = 0, in_bandwidth = 0, out_bandwidth = 0) defaults to 32 clients and unbounded channels/bandwidth (0 = unlimited); create_mesh(unique_id) exists for mesh topology.
claims.locator: Method Descriptions for create_server and create_mesh; class description 'ENet only uses UDP, not TCP'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable API reference; default, not a tuned production value.

claims.statement: The MultiplayerAPI instance used by a scene branch can be replaced via SceneTree.set_multiplayer(), which the docs state allows running both client and server in the same scene; the default implementation is SceneMultiplayer and it can be extended with MultiplayerAPIExtension.
claims.locator: Class description of MultiplayerAPI

claims.statement: None of the Godot sources opened in this assignment document built-in client prediction, server reconciliation or server-side lag compensation in the high-level multiplayer API; the exact gap (what a shipping Godot title must implement itself) is unverified here.
claims.locator: Page sections: Mid-level abstraction, Hosting considerations, Initializing the network, Managing connections, Remote procedure calls (no prediction/lag-compensation section)
claims.context: Gap: absence of documentation is NOT evidence of absence. Needs a Godot proposal/issue or a shipping-title postmortem to state the gap precisely.

claims.statement: Godot 4.0 shipped a server-based navigation system ('Navigation Server-Based Navigation System') with extended complex navigation support, replacing the Godot 3 navigation node design.
claims.locator: Section 'Navigation' of the Godot 4.0 release announcement

claims.statement: NavigationServer3D manages maps, regions and agents; maps are divided into regions composed of navigation meshes, and two regions connect only if their edge vertices are closer than edge_connection_margin.
claims.locator: Class description of NavigationServer3D

claims.statement: NavigationServer changes are not applied immediately: setters and deletes are queued and synchronised in the middle of the physics frame, so path queries in the same frame can return empty or stale results and code must await get_tree().physics_frame after setup.
claims.locator: Sections 'Threading and Synchronization' and 'Waiting for synchronization'

claims.statement: The NavigationServer uses a threadpool by default for some functionality such as avoidance calculation between agents, and the number of threads that can run simultaneously on map data is controlled by the project setting Navigation > Pathfinding > Max Threads.
claims.locator: Section 'Navigation' of 'Thread-safe APIs'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; no thread-count default is given.

claims.statement: NavigationServer3D is marked 'Experimental: This class may be changed or removed in future versions' in the API reference, and its collision avoidance ignores regions, so applying the returned velocity directly can push an agent outside the traversable area.
claims.locator: Class description: Experimental marker and the Note beginning 'The collision avoidance system ignores regions'

claims.statement: Navigation map data is thread-safe but not thread-friendly: NavigationSourceGeometryData, NavigationMesh and NavigationPolygon use internal read-write locks, so editing the same large navmesh from several threads causes thread congestion; AStar2D/3D/Grid2D are not thread-safe at all and two threads on the same AStar object corrupt data.
claims.locator: Section 'Navigation' of 'Thread-safe APIs'

claims.statement: Automatic occlusion culling was introduced in Godot 4.0: the release announcement describes it as detecting models hidden by other geometry and dynamically removing them to increase both CPU and GPU rendering performance, while noting it helps little in open environments.
claims.locator: Section on occlusion culling / mesh LOD in the Godot 4.0 release announcement

claims.statement: Godot's occlusion culling rasterises the scene's occluder geometry to a low-resolution buffer on the CPU using the Embree software raytracing library, then tests each occludee's AABB against the occluder shapes; an occludee's AABB must be FULLY occluded by the occluder shape to be culled.
claims.locator: Section 'How occlusion culling works in Godot'

claims.statement: Setup requires enabling Rendering > Occlusion Culling > Use Occlusion Culling (applies immediately, no editor restart), then adding an OccluderInstance3D node and using 'Bake Occluders', which produces an Occluder3D resource; Bake > Cull Mask can exclude visual layers (e.g. dynamic objects) from baking.
claims.locator: Section 'Setting up occlusion culling' and its subsections

claims.statement: Only MeshInstance3D nodes are taken into account when baking occluders; MultiMeshInstance3D, GPUParticles3D, CPUParticles3D and CSG nodes are not, so they must be approximated with manually created occluder shapes; since Godot 4.4 CSG nodes can participate if converted to MeshInstance3D first. The restriction does not apply to occludees.
claims.locator: Note under 'Automatically baking occluders (recommended)'

claims.statement: Occlusion culling adds CPU cost (occluder rasterisation plus per-occludee AABB tests), so the docs warn that 'in scenes with few occlusion culling opportunities, occlusion culling may not be worth the added setup and CPU usage'; the largest gains are in indoor scenes with many small rooms and, because the Mobile renderer has no depth prepass while Forward+ does, occlusion culling actively reduces shading overdraw on the Mobile renderer.
claims.locator: Sections 'Why use occlusion culling' and 'Performance considerations'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; qualitative, no ms figures.

claims.statement: The occlusion culling system is 'mostly static': moving or hiding OccluderInstance3D nodes at run time triggers a background recomputation that can take several frames, so the API reference recommends moving them only sporadically (e.g. procedural generation) rather than every frame.
claims.locator: Class description of OccluderInstance3D

claims.statement: PhysicsServer3D is the low-level 3D physics interface: a space is a self-contained simulation world containing bodies, areas and joints; a shape is a geometric primitive added to a body/area possibly with a local transform; a body can be static, kinematic or rigid; an area detects entering/exiting bodies and areas; a joint constrains one or two bodies. Physics objects may be created and manipulated without any scene-tree node.
claims.locator: Class description of PhysicsServer3D

claims.statement: Godot's whole scene system is optional and is built on servers (RenderingServer, PhysicsServer3D, PhysicsServer2D, AudioServer, ...); direct server use is reached through RIDs, which are opaque handles allocated and freed manually, and a resource's RID is NOT counted for reference-counting lifetime, so the resource must be kept referenced outside the server or both are erased.
claims.locator: Sections 'Servers' and 'RIDs' (including the Warning about RID references)

claims.statement: The server API path trades the scene layer's convenience for cost: the docs list the scene system's drawbacks as an extra layer of complexity, lower performance than using simple APIs directly, inability to use multiple threads to control them, and more memory needed - which is the price paid when bypassing it.
claims.locator: Section 'Optimization using Servers' (bullet list of drawbacks)

claims.statement: Physics simulation is not thread-safe by default; running the physics servers on separate threads requires enabling Physics > 2D > Run on Separate Thread and/or Physics > 3D > Run on Separate Thread, which is what makes the servers thread-safe.
claims.locator: Section 'Physics' of 'Thread-safe APIs'

claims.statement: Godot 4.4+ can interpolate transforms between physics ticks: enable Project Settings > Physics > Common > Physics Interpolation, keep (almost) all game logic in _physics_process rather than _process, and the docs suggest temporarily setting Physics Tick per Second to a low value such as 10 to expose interpolation problems.
claims.locator: Sections 'Turn on the physics interpolation setting' and 'Move (almost) all game logic from _process to _physics_process'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; 10 is the recommended debugging value, not a production setting.

claims.statement: Godot's built-in profiler is off by default because 'profiling is performance-intensive'; it is opened from the Debugger panel's Profiler tab and can be set to Autostart (a state that is not preserved across editor sessions).
claims.locator: Section 'An overview of the profiler'

claims.statement: The profiler's main measurements are frame time (all logic from physics to rendering), physics frame, idle time (non-physics logic such as _process, timers and Idle-updating cameras) and physics time; frame time includes rendering time, so particle or VFX spikes can appear as lag even when scripts and physics are fast.
claims.locator: Section 'The measured data'

claims.statement: The documented frame-time reference is 16.66 milliseconds by default, which corresponds to 60 FPS, and the physics frame is the time Godot has allocated between physics updates.
claims.locator: Section 'The measured data', paragraph on 'Physics frame'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; this is the default 60 FPS budget reference, not a measurement of any game.

claims.statement: The built-in profiler does not currently support C# scripts; the docs direct C# users to JetBrains Rider and dotTrace with the Godot support plugin.
claims.locator: Note under 'An overview of the profiler'

claims.statement: For runtime instrumentation the Performance singleton exposes the same monitors as the Debugger's Monitor tab (TIME_FPS, TIME_PROCESS, TIME_PHYSICS_PROCESS, TIME_NAVIGATION_PROCESS, memory, draw calls, ...) and allows adding custom monitors; some built-in monitors are debug-only and return 0 in release exports, and some are not updated in real time, with 'a delay of up to 1 second between changes'.
claims.locator: Class description and Notes; Monitor enum members

claims.statement: DirectionalLight3D shadows use Parallel Split Shadow Maps: the view frustum is split into 2 or 4 areas, each with its own shadow map, and the default shadow mode when shadows are enabled is PSSM with 4 splits. An object large enough to appear in all four splits is rendered five times in total - once per split plus once for the final scene rendering.
claims.locator: Section 'Directional shadow mapping'
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; the 'five times' figure is stated explicitly for that case.

claims.statement: With all rendering methods, up to 8 DirectionalLights can be visible at a time, and each additional DirectionalLight with shadows enabled reduces the effective shadow resolution of every DirectionalLight because the directional shadow atlas is shared between all lights; exceeding the limit makes lights pop in and out during camera movement.
claims.locator: Paragraph preceding 'Shadow mapping' (up to 8 DirectionalLights, shared directional shadow atlas)

claims.statement: The documented shadow controls are Shadow > Max Distance (lower values give better-looking shadows and better performance because fewer objects enter shadow rendering), Fade Start, Blend Splits (smoother transitions at the cost of detail and performance), Normal Bias (preferred over Bias for fixing acne), and split_1/split_2/split_3 distances.
claims.locator: Section 'Directional shadow mapping' and 'Tweaking shadow bias'

claims.statement: DirectionalLight3D exposes three shadow modes: SHADOW_ORTHOGONAL (0, 'the fastest directional shadow mode', may blur close objects), SHADOW_PARALLEL_2_SPLITS (1, compromise) and SHADOW_PARALLEL_4_SPLITS (2, 'the slowest directional shadow mode'); it also exposes directional_shadow_max_distance, fade_start, pancake_size, split_1..3 and blend_splits.
claims.locator: Enum ShadowMode and the property list of DirectionalLight3D

claims.statement: Setting Angular Distance above 0.0 on a directional light enables a contact-hardening shadow (PCSS) which softens shadows with distance; the docs state this kind of shadow is expensive and give the Sun's angular distance viewed from Earth as approximately 0.5 degrees for reference.
claims.locator: Section 'Directional light', paragraph on the Angular Distance property
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; 0.5 degrees is the real-world Sun reference value, not a recommended setting.

claims.statement: Godot ships two threading facilities: the Thread class, where start() launches a callable and wait_to_finish() must always be called to collect and dispose of the thread, and the WorkerThreadPool singleton, which allocates worker threads at project startup and accepts regular tasks (add_task) or group tasks (add_group_task) that distribute a callable over many elements.
claims.locator: Sections 'Threads' and 'Creating a Thread'; cross-referenced in SRC-GCS-020 class description

claims.statement: Creating threads is 'a slow operation, especially on Windows', so the docs advise creating threads before heavy processing (e.g. while a level loads) instead of just-in-time, and warn that locking and unlocking mutexes is also expensive, so locks should be held briefly and rarely.
claims.locator: Warning block in 'Creating a Thread' and the following paragraph on mutexes
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs; qualitative, no measured overhead.

claims.statement: The WorkerThreadPool API reference warns that using the singleton 'could affect performance negatively if the task being distributed between threads is not computationally expensive', and that a group task's element count must remain constant during the multithreaded part.
claims.locator: Note in the class description; Note in the add_group_task example

claims.statement: add_group_task(action, elements, tasks_needed = -1, high_priority = false, description = ''): the default tasks_needed = -1 distributes the task to all worker threads; tasks may be flagged high or low priority; every task must eventually be waited for with wait_for_task_completion() or wait_for_group_task_completion() so resources allocated inside it are cleaned up.
claims.locator: Method Descriptions for add_group_task and add_task, and their Warning

claims.statement: Thread safety is opt-in and partial: interacting with the active scene tree is not thread-safe (use call_deferred/set_deferred), instancing nodes that render in 2D or 3D is not thread-safe by default, and running the rendering driver on a separate thread requires Rendering > Driver > Thread Model = Separate - which the docs say 'has several known bugs, so it may not be usable in all scenarios'.
claims.locator: Sections 'Scene tree' and 'Rendering' of 'Thread-safe APIs'

claims.statement: Godot 4.0 shipped a dedicated 'Multithreading & Performance Optimization' workstream as part of the release, but the opened sources do not state the exact version in which WorkerThreadPool was first introduced.
claims.locator: Section heading 'Multithreading & Performance Optimization' in the Godot 4.0 release announcement
claims.context: Version attributed to the Godot 4.0 release post; the specific introduction version of WorkerThreadPool itself remains unverified.

claims.statement: Manual HLOD with full control over visibility ranges is presented in the Godot 4.0 release announcement alongside the new automatic occlusion culling and automatic mesh LOD, as the third performance option for large 3D scenes.
claims.locator: Section on occlusion culling / mesh LOD / visibility ranges in the Godot 4.0 release announcement

claims.statement: Visibility ranges are configured per node on any GeometryInstance3D (MeshInstance3D, MultiMeshInstance3D, GPUParticles3D, CPUParticles3D, Label3D, Sprite3D, AnimatedSprite3D, CSGShape3D) using Begin and End distances measured to the centre of the instance's AABB, plus Begin Margin and End Margin which act as hysteresis or fade distance.
claims.locator: Sections 'How it works' and 'Visibility range properties'

claims.statement: The benefit of HLOD over a traditional LOD system is its hierarchical nature: one larger mesh can replace several smaller meshes so draw calls drop at distance, while culling opportunities are preserved up close; because ranges are per node, different node types can participate in one LOD system (e.g. MeshInstance3D up close, Sprite3D impostor at distance).
claims.locator: Section 'How it works'

claims.statement: Fade Mode Disabled uses hysteresis to switch LOD levels instantly and 'provides the best performance as it doesn't force rendering to become transparent during the fade transition', whereas Fade Mode Self and Dependencies use alpha blending and 'force transparent rendering on the object during its fade transition, so it has a performance impact'.
claims.locator: Section 'Fade mode'

claims.statement: Automatic mesh LOD and visibility ranges can be used at the same time, even on the same mesh: the docs recommend visibility ranges when artist-authored LOD meshes are needed and automatic mesh LOD when they are not.
claims.locator: Section 'See also' in 'Mesh level of detail (LOD)'

claims.statement: CryEngine's audio occlusion is a raycast model configured per entity: SoundObstructionType on AudioTriggerSpot, AudioAreaEntity and AudioAreaAmbience can be Ignore (the default), SingleRay or MultipleRay; Ignore applies no raycasts at all, and raycasts are skipped for entities that have no active playing audio trigger even when the type is SingleRay or MultipleRay.
claims.locator: Section 'Overview' of 'Audio & Occlusion' (SoundObstructionType property table and following paragraph)

claims.statement: A non-zero Occlusion value is set for a source whenever at least one cast ray hits a surface with non-zero sound_obstruction; the per-surface sound_obstruction values are accumulated and averaged over time to produce that ray's Occlusion. With SingleRay the audio object's occlusion equals its only ray's value; with MultipleRay it is the average over all rays. Occlusion is applied before the environment aux buses, so it affects both dry and wet signal.
claims.locator: Section 'Sound Obstruction/Occlusion' -> 'Occlusion'

claims.statement: s_OcclusionMaxDistance caps the distance beyond which obstruction/occlusion calculations are disabled; the manual's worked example 's_OcclusionMaxDistance = 150' causes the engine to calculate obstruction/occlusion for every active audio object within 150 m of the listener.
claims.locator: Section 'Sound Obstruction/Occlusion' -> 'Occlusion', s_OcclusionMaxDistance example
claims.context: CRYENGINE 5.x official manual; 150 m is the manual's example value, not a documented default.

claims.statement: Occlusion granularity can be overridden globally with s_OcclusionGlobalType (0 = audio-object-specific ray casting, 1 = all objects ignore ray casting, 2 = adaptive, 3/4/5 = low/medium/high granularity) and s_OcclusionHighDistance (default 10 m) is the distance within which occlusion uses the most sample points; s_OcclusionAccumulate selects whether encountered occlusion values are accumulated or only the highest is used.
claims.locator: Sections 's_OcclusionAccumulate', 's_OcclusionGlobalType', 's_OcclusionHighDistance'
claims.context: CRYENGINE 5.7 docs (mirror). 10 m is the documented default of s_OcclusionHighDistance.

claims.statement: Obstruction is only computed when SoundObstructionType is MultipleRay, because a single ray cannot differentiate obstruction from occlusion; obstruction is applied after and in addition to occlusion.
claims.locator: Section 'Obstruction'

claims.statement: No opened CryEngine source states the CPU cost of audio ray casting (rays per object, ms per frame, or object-count budgets) for occlusion; the exact cost envelope is unverified.
claims.locator: Page describes the model and CVars but contains no CPU/ms measurements
claims.context: Gap: needs a Crytek profiling talk or a CryEngine profiling guide with audio ray-cast numbers.

claims.statement: CryEngine's volumetric fog is voxel-based: volume textures act as a view-frustum-shaped voxel buffer storing incoming light and the properties of participating media, and the system handles sun with dynamic shadow, environment probes, ambient light, and regular lights with dynamic shadows, as well as variations in fog density, consistently for opaque and transparent materials.
claims.locator: Section 'Overview' of 'Volumetric Fog'

claims.statement: Volumetric fog is split in two: ray-marching volumetric fog covers the area near the camera and handles all light types and differing fog densities, while analytical volumetric fog covers everything else and handles sun light without dynamic shadow plus exponential height fog density.
claims.locator: Section 'Overview' -> 'Voxel-based Volumetric Fog consists of two parts'

claims.statement: Volumetric fog is enabled with the console variable e_VolumetricFog = 1 (console window or system.cfg); sun radial scattering is tuned with Anisotropy (atmosphere) (low values near 0.0 for atmospheric fog over the whole sky) and Anisotropy (radial) (high values near 1.0 for a bloom around the sun), blended by the Radial blend factor.
claims.locator: Sections 'Overview' (e_VolumetricFog) and 'Sun Radial Scattering Setup'

claims.statement: Procedural volumetric clouds render at reduced resolution: r_VolumetricClouds accepts 0 (disabled, default), 1 (enabled at 1/2 resolution) and 2 (enabled at 1/4 resolution), and clouds are generated from noise plus an artist volume texture and shaded by ray marching with physically plausible shading.
claims.locator: Sections 'Overview' and 'CVars' -> r_VolumetricClouds
claims.context: CRYENGINE 5.7 docs (mirror of official page id 25535467).

claims.statement: Cloud ray-marching cost is controlled by r_VolumetricCloudsRaymarchStepNum, whose default is 64 and whose acceptable range is 16 to 256 in multiples of 16; r_VolumetricCloudsShadowResolution defaults to 64; temporal and stereo reprojection are on by default; and at most 4 CloudBlocker entities can work simultaneously in a level.
claims.locator: Sections 'CloudBlocker entity' and 'CVars'
claims.context: CRYENGINE 5.7 docs (mirror). Values are documented defaults/ranges from Crytek.

claims.statement: CryEngine's Merged Mesh (MM) vegetation combines several subsystems - vegetation, physics, explosions, and localized and global wind - into one system, and because of its batching it allows individual blades of grass to be used instead of patches, increasing variation through more instances.
claims.locator: Section 'Overview' of 'Vegetation 02 Grass (Merged Meshes)'
claims.context: CRYENGINE 5.7 docs (secondary mirror of official page id 24285889).

claims.statement: Because MM works by large-scale batching, Crytek enforces a very simplistic geometric setup for the asset: 'Using the MM technology on a grass patch will work but at a great expense on performance', and the guidance is to keep geometry as simple as possible and only use MM on assets built to the specific setup.

claims.context: CRYENGINE 5.7 docs (mirror); qualitative, no vertex or instance budgets are given.

claims.statement: AutoMerged was initially implemented to reduce draw calls while keeping the flexibility to paint grass objects on any surface without being restricted to large grass patches; the engine merges multiple meshes within several sectors into single meshes in real time, as long as they use the same material with the same textures, which also removes the need for 'Fit to Terrain'/'AlignToTerrain' handling.
claims.locator: Section 'AutoMerged Vegetation' of 'Bending Setup'
claims.context: CRYENGINE 3.5+ official manual; names Crysis 3 as the origin of physically correct wind bending.

claims.statement: AutoMerged vegetation is switched on per object with the 'AutoMerged' checkbox in the vegetation properties, and its rendering can be toggled globally with e_MergedMeshes 0/1.
claims.locator: Section 'AutoMerged Vegetation' -> 'You can also enable/disable rendering of the objects with e_MergedMeshes 0/1'

claims.statement: Merged-mesh vegetation assets must use the Vegetation shader and the Vegetation surface type in the Material Editor; in Crytek's own grass tutorial the material uses 100% opacity with an AlphaTest of 40, diffuse colour pure white (255,255,255) and specular in the 40-60 range to stay inside the PBS pipeline.
claims.locator: Sections 'Material Settings' and 'Opacity Settings' of 'Vegetation 02 Grass (Merged Meshes)'

claims.statement: SVOGI is voxel ray tracing: a voxel representation of the scene geometry is prepared at run time, on the CPU, asynchronously and incrementally, and every frame the GPU traces thousands of rays through the voxels (and shadow maps) to gather occlusion and indirect lighting.
claims.locator: Section 'How It Works' of 'Voxel-Based Global Illumination (SVOGI)'

claims.statement: Crytek's documented SVOGI cost in the low-spec configuration (AO + Sun bounce, no point lights) is 3-4 ms of GPU time on Xbox One and 2-3 ms on an average PC; the fastest configuration, AO-only mode, costs less than 2 ms on Xbox One.
claims.locator: Section 'Performance' of 'Voxel-Based Global Illumination (SVOGI)'
claims.context: Crytek's own low-spec configuration, Xbox One and unspecified 'average PC', CRYENGINE 5.x. Not a measurement of any shipped title.

claims.statement: The older CRYENGINE 3 documentation gives 4-5 ms of GPU time on Xbox One and 2-3 ms on a 'good PC (GTX 780)' in the same low-spec configuration, with the AO-only mode at about 2.5 ms on Xbox One.
claims.locator: Section 'Performance' of the CRYENGINE 3 'Voxel-Based Global Illumination' page
claims.context: CRYENGINE 3 manual, 2013-era hardware (GTX 780); superseded by the CRYENGINE 5.x figures but shows the generation-to-generation spread.

claims.statement: Crytek lists SVOGI's current limitations as: large-scale AO and indirect shadows may be cast properly only by static geometry; GI is not working on some forward rendering components such as particles or water; and there are artifacts such as ghosting, aliasing and light leaking. The default configuration provides only diffuse GI - specular lighting still requires light probes.
claims.locator: Sections 'Current Limitations' and 'How It Works' (diffuse-only default)

claims.statement: SVOGI is tuned in Tools > Environment Editor > Constants > Total Illumination (and Total Illumination Advanced); documented parameters include Diffuse cone width (wider cones are faster but cause over-occlusion and more light leaking; narrow cones are slower and noisier), Cone max length in metres (shorter rays are faster), Min node size (smaller values give more detail but run slower and use more memory, and may require raising VoxelPoolResolution to avoid running out of voxel pool), Injection multiplier, Sky color multiplier, Low spec mode and Update geometry (forces a full re-voxelisation).
claims.locator: Parameter table under 'User Interface' of the CRYENGINE 3 SVOGI page
claims.context: CRYENGINE 3 manual; the same parameter family appears in the CRYENGINE 5.x Environment Editor.

claims.statement: SVOGI works without pre-baking and without manual setup of bounce lights or light volumes, and is documented as usable as an AO add-on to light probes or as a complete replacement for their diffuse contribution.
claims.locator: Sections 'Overview' and 'How It Works'

claims.statement: CryEngine supports three kinds of vegetation bending: Touch bending (physical movement from collision), Detail bending (physical movement from wind) and Automerged bending (a more physically accurate system reacting to wind and collisions with higher performance). Physically correct wind bending was added with Crysis 3 and CRYENGINE 3.5 and is activated by the 'AutoMerged' checkbox.
claims.locator: Section 'Overview' of 'Bending Setup'

claims.statement: Touch bending is a rope/bone setup based on UV instancing: leaves sharing the same UV space automatically inherit the joint setup from a 'master leaf', and joints are placed as helpers/dummies connected by the naming convention branch<j>_<n> (e.g. branch1_1, branch1_2, branch1_3). The engine interpolates between the dummies like a rope and weights all other vertices automatically.
claims.locator: Sections 'Overview', 'Setup of Instances (UV Layout)' and 'Joint Setup'/'Naming Convention' of 'Touch Bending'

claims.statement: Touch bending requires the object to have a volume proxy physicalised as 'noCollide'; touch bending is only detected inside this proxy. A newer, more optimised approach called merged mesh deform also exists, and the manual advises considering both techniques before applying.
claims.locator: Sections 'Volume Proxy' and 'Overview' ('newer versions of the engine actually feature a easier to use, more optimized approach known as merged mesh deform')

claims.statement: Detail and Touch bending are tuned with a single Bending property per vegetation object - the higher the value, the more strongly the object reacts to main bending - while AutoMerged vegetation exposes its own separate set of bending properties in the Sandbox Vegetation Tool.
claims.locator: Section 'Overview' of 'Bending Setup'
claims.context: CRYENGINE 3.5+ official manual; no numeric range is given.

claims.statement: The 5.7 merged-mesh documentation states that the batching technology forces a very simplistic geometric setup and that using MM on a grass patch 'will work but at a great expense on performance'; assets must be authored to the specific setup rather than adapted from arbitrary patches.

claims.statement: Source's client command is a per-tick CUserCmd carrying command_number, tick_count ('the tick the client created this command'), viewangles, forwardmove/sidemove/upmove, buttons, impulse, weaponselect, random_seed and a hasbeenpredicted flag; a CRC32 checksum is computed over exactly those fields so client and server commands can be matched.

claims.context: Public Source SDK 2013 header (Half-Life 2 / Source 1 branch).

claims.statement: Client-side prediction and server-side lag compensation are engine switches exposed as convars: cl_predictweapons defaults to 1 ('Perform client side prediction of weapon effects.') and cl_lagcompensation defaults to 1 ('Perform server side lag compensation of weapon firing events.'); the prediction system tracks m_nCommandsPredicted and m_nServerCommandsAcknowledged, and cl_pred_optimize defaults to 2, which avoids re-predicting when there were no errors and avoids copying data when no network update arrived.
claims.locator: Top-of-file ConVar declarations and CPrediction member initialisation in src/game/client/prediction.cpp
claims.context: Public Source SDK 2013 client code; these are engine defaults, not tuned per-title values.

claims.statement: Source's networked state uses data tables with hard limits: MAX_DATATABLES 1024 (documented as 'must be a power of 2'), MAX_DATATABLE_PROPS 4096, MAX_ARRAY_ELEMENTS 2048, and DT_MAX_STRING_BITS 9; individual properties can be encoded against the tick count via SPROP_ENCODED_AGAINST_TICKCOUNT, which is used for m_flAnimTime and m_flSimulationTime.
claims.locator: #define block at the top of src/public/dt_common.h and the comment above SPROP_ENCODED_AGAINST_TICKCOUNT
claims.context: Public Source SDK 2013 header; these are compile-time engine limits for the delta-compressed state model.

claims.statement: Valve has continued to extend sub-tick precision into individual gameplay systems: the 2026-01-21 patch note states 'Landing time is now calculated with subtick precision', and the 2025-09-17 note states 'Improved timestep-independence of subtick movement acceleration'.

claims.statement: Source's area-portal system is stored as explicit lumps: each area has a list of portals leading into other areas, and the header comment states that 'when portals are closed, other areas may not be visible or hearable even if the vis info says that it should be'. struct dareaportal_t carries m_PortalKey (bound to the entity's portalnumber), otherarea, portal geometry (m_FirstClipPortalVert, m_nClipPortalVerts) and planenum.

claims.statement: The BSP lump table enumerates the visibility-related data: LUMP_VISIBILITY = 4, LUMP_NODES = 5, LUMP_LEAFS = 10, LUMP_AREAS = 20 and LUMP_AREAPORTALS = 21, alongside geometry lumps (LUMP_FACES, LUMP_BRUSHES, LUMP_BRUSHSIDES).

claims.statement: bevy_tasks is a minimal threadpool whose main use case is scoped fork-join - spawning tasks from a single thread and having that thread await their completion - and it explicitly 'makes no attempt to ensure fairness or ordering of spawned tasks'.

claims.statement: Bevy separates work into three pools chosen by latency requirement: ComputeTaskPool and AsyncComputeTaskPool for CPU-intensive work (with work not needed for the next frame going to the async pool) and IoTaskPool for IO-intensive work whose tasks are expected to complete very quickly; the same API is used on single-threaded targets such as Wasm.
claims.locator: Section 'Usage' of crates/bevy_tasks/README.md

claims.statement: Godot's built-in equivalent is WorkerThreadPool: the singleton allocates worker threads at project startup and offers add_task for a single worker and add_group_task for work distributed across several workers, the latter being described as useful for 'iterating over a lot of elements, such as the enemies in an arena'.
claims.locator: Class description and add_group_task method description in the WorkerThreadPool class reference

claims.statement: Both reference engines warn about dispatch overhead: Godot states that creating threads is 'a slow operation, especially on Windows' and that locking/unlocking mutexes is expensive, and its WorkerThreadPool reference warns the singleton 'could affect performance negatively if the task being distributed between threads is not computationally expensive'.

claims.context: Godot 4.x stable API reference; cross-referenced with the thread-creation warning in SRC-GCS-016.

claims.statement: Godot's group-task distribution is controlled by tasks_needed (default -1 = distribute to all worker threads) with a high_priority flag, and every task must eventually be awaited with wait_for_task_completion() or wait_for_group_task_completion() so that resources allocated inside the task are cleaned up; the element count must stay constant during the multithreaded part.

claims.statement: FrameGraph is a render-graph layer for Vulkan that hides synchronisation, memory allocation and the boilerplate needed to get Vulkan working, and adds built-in validations alongside the Vulkan validation layers; it deliberately does not perform device initialisation or window creation, which must happen before the FrameGraph instance is created.

claims.statement: The graph's execution model is multithreaded command-buffer recording: features include 'multithreaded command buffer building and submission', support for async compute and async transfer queues, and 'all render tasks are stateless'; synchronisation is expressed by declaring dependencies between command buffers (AddDependency) before Execute, with Begin/Execute/Flush internally synchronised.
claims.locator: Section 'Features' of the FrameGraph README; 'CPU thread synchronization examples' in docs/Multithreading.md

claims.statement: FrameGraph exposes a data-race check for multithreaded renderers: defining FG_ENABLE_DATA_RACE_CHECK allows immediate detection of missed synchronisation (race conditions), which the documentation recommends whenever developing a multithreaded renderer with it.
claims.locator: Section 'Validation' of docs/Multithreading.md

claims.statement: Resource lifetime in the graph is tied to submitted command buffers: resources are created through the graph (CreateImage/CreateBuffer), captured by command buffers via AddTask, and released with ReleaseResource; the resource is destroyed when the referencing command buffers complete (Wait), so the graph owns transient-resource lifetime.
claims.locator: Section 'Resource creation and destruction.' of docs/Multithreading.md

claims.statement: The graph relies on modern explicit-API features rather than hiding them: push constants, dynamic buffer offset, specialization constants, VK_EXT_descriptor_indexing, VK_NV_mesh_shader, VK_NV_shading_rate_image, VK_NV_ray_tracing and VK_KHR_shader_clock; shader compilation is delegated to a separate pipeline-compiler extension that accepts VKSL/SPIRV/GLSL formats.

claims.locator: Architecture list and the 'High-Level Features' bullet for the Resource Loader in the The Forge README

claims.statement: Godot's streaming primitive is ResourceLoader background loading: load_threaded_request queues a path for threaded loading, load_threaded_get_status reports ThreadLoadStatus (THREAD_LOAD_INVALID_RESOURCE=0, IN_PROGRESS=1, FAILED=2, LOADED=3) with progress as a one-element percentage array, and load_threaded_get retrieves the resource.
claims.locator: Section 'Using ResourceLoader'; enum ThreadLoadStatus in the ResourceLoader class reference
claims.context: Godot 4.x stable docs and API reference.

claims.statement: Streaming behaviour is controlled by two parameters of load_threaded_request: use_sub_threads (default false - using multiple threads speeds loading but may affect the main thread) and cache_mode (default CACHE_MODE_REUSE=1), where the deep variants CACHE_MODE_IGNORE_DEEP=3 and CACHE_MODE_REPLACE_DEEP=4 propagate the choice recursively down the dependency tree.
claims.locator: Method description for load_threaded_request and enum CacheMode in the ResourceLoader class reference

claims.statement: The blocking hazard is documented: once load_threaded_get() is called it either returns instantly or blocks exactly like the synchronous load(), so guaranteeing a non-blocking load requires either enough time between request and retrieval or explicit status polling.
claims.locator: Section 'Using ResourceLoader', paragraph beginning 'Once you call load_threaded_get()'

claims.statement: Resource-level threading is constrained: modifying a unique resource from multiple threads is not supported, and the same resource must not be loaded from several threads at once, so the documented pattern is one loading thread plus the main thread for adding to the active scene.
claims.locator: Section 'Resources' of 'Thread-safe APIs'

claims.statement: No source opened gives streaming budgets - throughput in MB/s, per-frame upload caps, or the resident memory cost of a streaming pool - for any of these engines; the streaming memory envelope is unverified.
claims.locator: The Forge README documents the loader's existence, not its throughput or memory behaviour
claims.context: Gap: needs a platform-holder streaming guide or a title postmortem with I/O and memory numbers. applicability_note: reference implementations are frameworks/engines, so their behaviour is a design reference only.
